stem: A company runs a managed relational database for an order system in one AWS Region. The database must lose no committed write if an Availability Zone fails. If the whole Region fails, the company must be able to recover the database in a second Region, and a loss of a few minutes of writes is acceptable. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: lose no committed write if an Availability Zone fails
a loss of a few minutes of writes is acceptable

options.text: Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with synchronous replication from the primary database.
options.why: The zones of a Region are close enough to [replicate data synchronously between Availability Zones](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-latency-single-digit-ms), so the standby holds every committed write.

options.text: Take a snapshot of the database every few minutes, and keep all of the snapshots in the same AWS Region as the database.
options.why: The snapshots stay in the failed Region, because no copy exists in another Region [unless you explicitly use a replication or copy feature offered by an AWS service or replicate the resource yourself](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-automatic-cross-region-replication).

options.text: Keep a replica of the database in a second AWS Region, with asynchronous replication from the primary database in the first Region.
options.why: The Region copy is asynchronous, and the stem accepts [the possibility of data loss or inconsistency when you fail over](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-async-cross-region-replication-may-lose-data) of a few minutes.

options.text: Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with asynchronous replication every few minutes.
options.why: Asynchronous replication can leave the newest writes behind, so a zone failure can lose committed writes that the stem does not allow.
options.misconception: Any copy in a second zone protects every committed write.

options.text: Run a self-managed database on EC2 instances in a second AWS Region, and write a custom process that ships the changes every minute.
options.why: It can meet the few minutes of loss, but a self-managed database and a custom process add far more operational work than a managed replica.

explanation: Two failures need two copies. The zones are close enough to [replicate data synchronously between Availability Zones](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-latency-single-digit-ms), so the standby keeps every committed write. The replica in a second Region is asynchronous, which the stem accepts.
takeaway: Synchronous standby in a second zone for zero loss; asynchronous replica in a second Region for a short loss.
twin: If the stem said "a Region failure must lose no committed write" instead: the asynchronous replica no longer meets it, because it brings [the possibility of data loss or inconsistency when you fail over](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-async-cross-region-replication-may-lose-data).
say: Synchronous to a second zone for zero loss, asynchronous to a second Region with a few minutes of loss.
